extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of literature interested in poetic theory and style
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance on how the language and construction of metrical poetry differ from prose — origins and elements of metre, appropriate diction for poetry, and how metre imposes conditions on choice and ordering of words. Aimed at critics and practicing poets judging or composing serious poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential difference between prose and metrical composition
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an essential difference (in the sense of contra-distinction) between the formal construction/architecture of poetic language and that of prose; modes of expression, construction, order of sentences, and use/frequency of figures can be appropriate to one and vicious or heterogeneous in the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The true question is not whether some sentences may suit both verse and prose, but whether there are arrangements of words, figures, and sentence-orders proper to poetry but unsuitable to prose, and vice versa. Coleridge argues that such unfitness often exists and ought to be recognized; he supports this by appeal to origin of metre, effects of metre, poetic practice (Homer to Milton) and examples (Gray's sonnet, Spenser, Daniel, Milton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Replace equivocal 'real' with 'ordinary' (lingua communis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'real' (as used to claim a poet adopts the language of a class) is equivocal; one should speak of ordinary language or lingua communis, which is not identical with the phraseology of any single low or rustic class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every man's language has individualities, class-properties, and universal words; the ordinary/common language is not the exclusive property of rustics. Therefore poetry cannot claim to adopt a 'real' rustic language without substantial omissions and changes; provincialisms must be removed and order adjusted before rustic speech can serve general poetic purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rustic speech varies and is not a universal model
rubrics_metrics.description: The rustic language highly extolled by some poets varies in every county and village and depends on local factors (clergyman, schools, politics, newspapers); anterior to cultivation lingua communis exists in parts and nowhere whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of local variability, adopting 'the language of rustic life' as a universal poetic model is impracticable and would require numerous weighty omissions and changes to function in most poetic forms (except drama or professed imitation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Passion does not create vocabulary; language of excitement depends on prior store
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a person is strongly affected, the nature of his words depends on the number and quality of conceptions and images and the words expressing them which his mind had previously stored; passion sets faculties in increased activity but does not create terms ex nihilo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New connections or generalizations produced by passion must be conveyed with pre-existing terms; certain conversational fillers and repetitions of an uncultivated speaker may be copied into poetry but generally are of little assistance or ornament to a poem (exceptions: high repetitions in sustained passion, e.g., Deborah's song).

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of metre: balance of passion and will
rubrics_metrics.description: Metre originates from a mental balance effected to hold in check the workings of passion; that antagonism, assisted by the state it counteracts, became organized into metre by a supervening act of will and judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From this origin Coleridge deduces two critic-expectable conditions in metrical work: (1) the metre should be accompanied by the natural language of excitement; (2) the marks/traces of present volition should be proportionably discernible throughout the metrical language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union/interpenetration of spontaneous passion and voluntary purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Metrical language requires a reconciled union of passion (spontaneous impulse) and will (voluntary purpose); both must be co-present and interpenetrate in the poem's diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This union manifests in more frequent employment of certain forms and figures (originally born of passion but adopted by power). There is a tacit compact between poet and reader: the poet supplies, and the reader expects, a particular species and degree of pleasurable excitement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency and kinds of figures of speech in poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry will employ picturesque and vivifying language, and certain figures of speech, with a frequency and in kinds/occasions greater than would be appropriate in serious prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because metre encourages sustained excitement and voluntary embellishment, critics should expect a higher rate of figurative language in poetry; such frequency would be excessive or alien in non-metrical prose on equal subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre as stimulant requires appropriate material
rubrics_metrics.description: Metre in itself is a stimulant of attention (increasing vivacity and susceptibility by surprise and re-excited curiosity), and thus requires appropriate matter and expressions to satisfy the attention it arouses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If metre rouses attention but suitable corresponding food (ideas, images, expressions) is not provided, a disappointment results. Metre is like yeast: worthless or disagreeable by itself but giving vivacity when proportionally combined with proper material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre alone insufficient—must combine with other poetic elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Metre's pleasurable effects are conditional on its combination with suitable elements of poetry; metre without compatible diction/thoughts often becomes feeble or absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge argues from examples (some stanzas in Wordsworth feel oddly metrical despite colloquial diction) that metre should not be used merely for its own sake and that some pieces might be better in prose (e.g., certain anecdotes and tales).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry implies an excited state of feeling (passion) and thus different diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry always implies passion (understood generally as an excited state of feelings and faculties), and the act of composing poetry itself produces an unusual state of excitement that justifies and demands a corresponding difference of language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The vividness of poetic description can derive as much from the describer's force as from subject matter; this heightened state legitimates poetic forms, epithets, and arrangements not typical of prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order/prospectiveness of diction distinguishes educated from uneducated speech
rubrics_metrics.description: In uneducated intercourse there is greater disjunction and a lack of prospectiveness (foresight of the whole to subordinate parts) compared with the diction of the educated; the poetic writer must exercise prospectiveness to subordinate and arrange parts as an organized whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere adoption of rustic words without their ordering will not reproduce the poetic diction of the class; poets must select and arrange words by judgment, unlike the loose succession often found in rustic speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid incongruous personification and muddled images
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic diction should not substitute incongruous images or confused personifications that conflate cause and effect or the real thing with a personified representative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faulty lines (example: 'And reddening Phoebus lifts his golden fire') are bad not because they differ from prose but because they convey incongruous images or bad sense. Such faults are accidental and age-dependent (hackneyed classical images), not structural objections to poetic diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical mnemonic function of metre is not sole defence of its poetic status
rubrics_metrics.description: Before printing and writing, metre (including alliteration and rhyme) had independent value in aiding recollection and preservation of tales and truths, but this historical role does not by itself justify metre's modern poetic use or account for all popular retention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many popular tales have persisted in prose (Tom Hickathrift, Jack the Giant-Killer), showing metre is not the only or decisive factor in preservation; therefore evaluate metre's utility relative to content and audience, not merely tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some works are better in prose than metrical form
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain narratives or pieces, even though poetically conceived, might be more delightful or fitting in prose; metre can sometimes produce oddity when set to colloquial, highly conversational diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge cites Sterne's Maria, The Monk, The Poor Man's Ass, and Wordsworth's Anecdote for Fathers, Simon Lee, Beggars, etc., as pieces that could be more effective in prose; critics should judge whether metre enhances or detracts from the material.
